subject: chemistry
question_text: State Fajan's rules and give suitable examples.

verification.note: Chapter 3 is sourced from the Sri Chaitanya Junior Fastrack chemistry section (book pp.56-61), which prints the question, its star rank and a model answer. Only ONE source book is held for chemistry — the TSBIE Basic Learning Material in hand covers physics only — so the two-book union check is PENDING a second chemistry source. The 1+1+1+1 mark split is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it; the question itself is sourced, not invented. The book states each rule in its ionic-increase direction; the card states both directions of each rule, which is the form the comparison questions use.

steps.label: Cation size rule
lines: Fajan's rules predict the nature (ionic or
covalent) of the bond between two atoms.
1. As the size of the cation increases, the
ionic nature of the bond increases.
A small cation gives more covalent nature.
Ex: cation size Li⁺ < Na⁺ < K⁺ < Rb⁺ < Cs⁺,
so ionic nature
LiCl < NaCl < KCl < RbCl < CsCl.
steps.why: A small cation has a concentrated positive charge, so it distorts (polarises) the anion's electron cloud more, pulling shared character into the bond. A large cation distorts less, so the bond stays more ionic.
common_mistakes: Reversing the series: LiCl is the MOST covalent chloride here, CsCl the most ionic.
Stating the rule without its example series. The series is half the mark.
steps.memory_tip: Small cation, strong distortion, covalent. Large cation, weak distortion, ionic.
steps.margin_note: Open with the one-line purpose of the rules, then number each rule.

steps.label: Anion size rule
lines: 2. As the size of the anion decreases, the
ionic nature of the bond increases.
A large anion gives more covalent nature.
Ex: anion size F⁻ < Cl⁻ < Br⁻ < I⁻,
so ionic nature
CaF₂ > CaCl₂ > CaBr₂ > CaI₂.
steps.why: A large anion's outer electrons are far from its nucleus and easily distorted toward the cation, so the bond gains covalent character. A small anion is distorted least.
common_mistakes: Writing the calcium series with < signs. Ionic nature DECREASES from fluoride to iodide, so the signs are >.
Mixing this up with the cation rule: for anions, SMALL means more ionic.
steps.memory_tip: For anions it is the reverse of cations: the small anion keeps the bond ionic.
steps.margin_note: Give both series: the ion sizes and the resulting ionic order.

steps.label: Charge rule
lines: 3. As the charge on the cation or the anion
decreases, the ionic nature of the bond
increases; high charge gives covalent
nature.
Ex: NaCl is ionic (small charge on Na⁺),
but AlCl₃ is covalent (high charge on Al³⁺).
steps.why: A highly charged cation polarises the anion strongly, so charge acts the same way as small size: more distortion, more covalent character.
common_mistakes: Saying higher charge means more ionic. Higher charge means MORE polarisation, so more covalent.
Writing the aluminium ion as Al⁺. It is Al³⁺, and the 3 is the point of the example.
steps.memory_tip: High charge acts like small size: both distort the anion, and distortion gives covalent character.
steps.margin_note: NaCl against AlCl₃ is the expected pair.

steps.label: Configuration rule
lines: 4. A cation with an inert gas configuration
forms an ionic compound; a cation with a
pseudo inert gas configuration forms a
covalent compound.
Ex: NaCl is ionic — Na⁺ is (2, 8);
ZnCl₂ is covalent — Zn²⁺ is (2, 8, 18).

lines.text: Small cation, large anion, high charge → covalent

steps.why: The 18 outer electrons of a pseudo inert gas cation shield its nucleus poorly, so it polarises the anion more than a true noble gas cation of similar size and charge.
common_mistakes: Writing Zn²⁺ as (2, 8, 8, 2). The ion is (2, 8, 18).
Leaving out the boxed summary line, which is the one-line version examiners reward.
steps.memory_tip: This rule reuses the Ca²⁺ against Zn²⁺ comparison: true noble gas ionic, pseudo covalent.
steps.margin_note: Close with the boxed one-line summary of all four rules.

insider_note: Each rule earns its mark only with its example series — learn the four pairs, rule with example, as single units.
